newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss money-laundering law moves closer to passage.
newsitem.headline: Swiss money-laundering law moves closer to passage.

text.p: A draft Swiss law aimed at cracking down on money-laundering by requiring banks and all other money managers to report suspicious transactions was passed on Wednesday by a key Swiss parliament committee.
The lower chamber's legal committee unanimously backed the government bill that also extends existing rules against money-laundering from banks to all other professional money managers.

"The bill will create a unitary standard of diligence for the whole financial sector and monitor compliance," a committee statement said, adding the legislation would go to the lower chamber's plenum for a vote in the 1997 spring session.

Switzerland, under international pressure to help crack down on profits from organised crime, in 1994 curtailed the country's legendary bank secrecy for the first time with a law allowing banks to report suspicious customers to police.
But the draft law goes further by requiring bankers, asset managers and lawyers to blow the whistle if they suspect money is coming from the drugs trade or other mafia-style crime.
Critics, including many in the banking and financial services sectors, have said the law's reporting requirements were too sweeping and that they would needlessly foster bureaucracy.

The bill offered by the Federal Council, or cabinet, last July also extends existing rules on money-laundering from banks to the large sector of non-bank asset managers, such as investment funds, life insurers and financial trustees.
These provisions include police powers to freeze suspicious assets pending an investigation, and requirements that money managers keep a paper trail on financial transactions.
